transcript.text: Excuse me.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Yes?
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: I wonder if you could spare a few minutes to do a survey on transport.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: It won’t take long.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: No, that’s fine.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Lovely.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: The survey is on behalf of the local council.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: They’d like to know about what transport you use any suggestions for improvement.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Can I start by asking you how you travelled to town today?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: I came on the bus.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Now can I get a few details about yourself?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: What’s your name?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: It’s Luisa …
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Hardie.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Can you spell that, please?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Yes, it’s H-A-R-D-I-E.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And can I have your address?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: It’s 19, White Stone Road.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Oh, right.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: I know that area.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: It’s Bradfield, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Is the postcode GT7?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: It’s actually G-T-8, 2-L-C.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And could I ask what your job is?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Are you a student?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: I’ve actually just finished my training.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: I’m a hairdresser.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Oh, right.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And one more question in this section.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: What is the reason for you coming into town today?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Actually it’s not for shopping today, which would be my normal reason, but to see the dentist.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Now in this last section I’d like you to give us some ideas about the facilities and arrangements in the city for getting to and from work, er, any suggestions you have for improvements.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Well, something I’ve thought about for some time is that when I do walk and I’m doing a later shift, I think the lighting should be better.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Yes, good point.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And of course, I think it’s a real shame they’ve been cutting down on the number of footpaths.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: They should have more of those.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Then people would walk more.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Yes, right.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And, I don’t think there are enough trains.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: That’s why I don’t use them – you have to wait so long.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And finally I’d like to ask your opinion on cycling.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: As you may know, there’s a drive in the city to get more people to cycle to work.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: But we realise that there are things which the council, but also employers, might do to help encourage workers to cycle to work.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Yep.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Well, I have thought about it and where I work there are no safe places to leave your bikes.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And also, I’d have to cycle uphill and on a hot day I’d arrive at work pretty sweaty so I think I’d need a shower somewhere at work.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: And I suppose the last thing is that I wouldn’t be all that confident about cycling on such busy roads.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: I think I’d like to see you offering training for that, you know.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: I’d feel a lot better about starting if that was the case.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Well, that’s very helpful.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Thank you very much for your time.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: No problem.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Bye.
transcript.speaker: LUISA

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: I’m very pleased to have this opportunity to say a little about two exciting new developments in the city: the Brackenside Open-Air Swimming Pool and the children’s Adventure Playground in Central Park.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: As many of you may know, the idea for these initiatives came from you, the public, in the extensive consultation exercise which the City Council conducted last year.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: And they have been realised using money from the SWRDC – the South West Regional Development Commission.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: First of all, Brackenside Pool.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: As many of the older members of the audience will remember, there used to be a wonderful open-air pool on the sea front 30 years ago but it had to close when it was judged to be unsafe.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: For the design of this new heated pool, we were very happy to secure the talents of internationally renowned architect Ellen Wendon, who has managed to combine a charming 1930s design, which fits in so well with many of the other buildings in the area, with up-to-the-minute features such as a recycling system – the only one of its kind in the world – which enables seawater to be used in the pool.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Now, there has been quite a bit of discussion in the local press about whether there would be enough room for the number of visitors we’re hoping to attract, but the design is deceptive and there have been rigorous checks about capacity.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Also, just in case you were wondering, we’re on schedule for a June 15th opening date and well within budget: a testimony to the excellent work of local contractors Hickman’s.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: We hope that as many people as possible will be there on June 15th.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: We have engaged award-winning actress Coral White to declare the pool open and there’ll be drinks and snacks available at the pool side.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: There’ll also be a competition for the public to decide on the sculpture we plan to have at the entrance: you will decide which famous historical figure from the city we should have.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: And now, moving on the Central Park Playground, which we’re pleased to announce has just won the Douglas Award for safety: the news came through only last week.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: The unique design is based on the concept of the Global Village, with the playground being divided into sex areas showing different parts of the world – each with a representative feature.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: For example, there is a section on Asia, and this is represented by rides and equipment in the shape of snakes, orang-utans, tigers and so on – fauna native to the forests of the region.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Moving south to the Antarctic – we couldn’t run to an ice rink I’m afraid but opted instead for climbing blocks in the shape of mountains – I thought they could have had slides for the glaciers but the designers did want to avoid being too literal!
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Then on to South America – and here the theme is El Dorado – games replicating the search for mines full of precious stones.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: And then moving up to North America, here there was considerable debate – I know the contribution of cinema and jazz was considered but the designers finally opted for rockets and the international Space Station.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Eastwards to Europe then, and perhaps the most traditional choice of all the areas: medieval castles and other fortifications.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Then last, but not least, moving south to Africa and a whole set of wonderful mosaics and trails to represent the great rivers of this fascinating and varied continent.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Now, the opening date for our Global Playground is 10th July.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: And again we’d love to see you there – so make a date and come and see this magnificent, original new amenity right in the heart of the city.
transcript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

transcript.text: Right, well, for our presentation shall I start with the early life of Thor Heyerdahl?
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Why don’t you begin with describing the type of boy he was, especially his passion for collecting things.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: That’s right, he had his own little museum.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: And I think it’s unusual for children to develop their own values and not join in their parents’ hobbies; I’m thinking of how Heyerdahl wouldn’t go hunting with his dad, for example.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Yeah, he preferred to learn about nature by listening to his mother read to him.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: And quite early on he knew he wanted to become an explorer when he grew up.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: That came from his camping trips he went on in Norway I think …
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: No, it was climbing that he spent his time on as a young man.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Oh, right … After university he married a classmate and together, they decided to experience living on a small island, to find out how harsh weather conditions shaped people’s lifestyles.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: As part of their preparation before they left home, they learnt basic survival skills like building a shelter.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: I guess they needed that knowledge in order to live wild in a remote location with few inhabitants, cut off by the sea, which is what they were aiming to do.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: An important part of your talk should be the radical theory Heyerdahl formed from examining mysterious ancient carvings that he happened to find on the island.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: I think you should finish with that.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: All right, Victor, so after your part I’ll talk about Thor Heyerdahl’s adult life, continuing from the theory he had about Polynesian migration: Up until that time of course, academics had believed that humans first migrated to the islands in Polynesia from Asia, in the west.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Yes, they thought that travel from the east was impossible, because of the huge, empty stretch of ocean that lies between the islands and the nearest inhabited land.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Yes, but Heyerdahl spent ages studying the cloud movements, ocean currents and wind patterns to find if it was actually possible.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: And another argument was that there was no tradition of large ship-building in the communities lying to the east of Polynesia.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: But Heyerdahl knew they made lots of coastal voyages in locally built canoes.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Yes, or sailing on rafts, as was shown by the long voyage that Heyerdahl did next.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: It was an incredibly risky journey to undertake – sometimes I wonder if he did that trip for private reasons, you know?
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: To show others that he could have spectacular adventures.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: What do you think, Olivia?
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Well, I think it was more a matter of simply trying out his idea, to see if migration from the east was possible.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Yes, that’s probably it.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: And the poor guy suffered a bit at that time because the war forced him to stop his work for some years …
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: When he got started again and planned his epic voyage, do you think it was important to him that he achieve it before anyone else did?
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Um, I haven’t read anywhere that that was his motivation.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: The most important factor seems to have been that he use only ancient techniques and local materials to build his raft.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: I wonder how fast it went.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Well, it took them 97 days from South America to the Pacific Island.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: And after that, Heyerdahl went to Easter Island, didn’t he?
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: We should mention the purpose of that trip.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: I think he sailed there in a boat made out of reeds.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: No, that was later on in Egypt, Olivia.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Oh, yes, that’s right.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: But what he wanted to do was talk to the local people about their old stone carvings and then make one himself to learn more about the process.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Well, what a great life.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Even though many of his theories have been disproven, he certainly left a lasting impression on many disciplines, didn’t he?
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: To my mind, he was first person to establish what modern academics call practical archaeology.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: I mean, that they try to recreate something from the past today, like he did with his raft trip.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: It’s unfortunate that his ideas about where Polynesians originated from have been completely discredited.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Right, well, I’ll prepare a PowerPoint slide at the end that acknowledges our sources.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: I mainly used The Life and Work of Thor Heyerdahl by William Oliver.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: I thought the research methods he used were very sound, although I must say I found the overall tone somewhat old-fashioned.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: I think they need to do a new, revised edition.
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: Yeah, I agree.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: What about the subject matter – I found it really challenging!
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Well, it’s a complex issue …
transcript.speaker: VICTOR

transcript.text: I thought the book had lots of good points.
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: What did you think of …
transcript.speaker: OLIVIA

transcript.text: Well, I’ve been talking to managers in a number of businesses, and reading surveys about the future of management.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And what I’m going to present in this seminar is a few ideas about how the activity is likely to change in the next ten years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It isn’t a scientific, statistical analysis – just some ideas for us to discuss.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One area I want to mention is business markets, and I’m sure a really significant development will be a major increase in competition, with companies from all round the world trying to sell similar products.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Consumers will have much more choice – for instance, food products sold in Australia might be manufactured in the USA, China, Finland and dozens of other countries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: At the same time, mergers and takeovers mean that governments are actually losing power to major global corporations.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: We can probably all think of companies that exert a great deal of influence, which may be good for consumers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: A third point I want to make about markets is that in the rapidly expanding economies, such as India, China, Brazil and Russia, demand is growing very fast.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is putting pressure on resources all over the world.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I think businesses are becoming more open to external influences.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In particular, companies are consulting customers more and more before making their business decisions.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Companies are finding out what they want and providing it, instead of making products and then trying to sell them, which is the model of years ago.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another influence is that concerns about the environment will force manufacturers to extend product lifecycles, to reduce the amount of pollution and waste.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And in some cases, regulation will need to be strengthened.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many societies are much more fluid and democratic, and the structure of companies is changing to reflect that.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I think we’re going to see a greater emphasis within companies on teams created with a specific project in mind.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And when they’re completed, the teams will be disbanded and new ones formed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: More and more people see work as simply one part of their lifestyle, and not the most important one, and as the workforce is shrinking in some countries, businesses are having to compete for staff instead of being about to choose among a lot of applicants.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Typical examples that will attract and retain staff are traditional ones like flexible hours and – something that has been made possible by advances in technology – remote working, with people based at their home, abroad, or almost anywhere they choose.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Management styles will almost certainly continue to change.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Senior managers will require a lot more than the efficiency that they’ve always needed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Above all they’ll need great skills in leadership, so that their organisation can initiate and respond to change in a fast-moving world, where they face lots of competing requirements and potential conflicts.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In most of the world, the senior managers of large businesses are mainly men in their fifties and sixties.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The predominant style of management will almost certainly become more consultative and collaborative, caused above all, by more women moving into senior management positions.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many of the changes are influenced by developments in the wider economy.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The traditional emphasis of business was manufacturing, and of course the service sector is very important.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But we shouldn’t overlook the growing financial contribution of IP, that is, intellectual property.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some books and films generate enormous sums from the sale of related DVDs, music, games, clothes, and so on.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another point I’d like to make is that although I’ve been talking about companies, one trend that they have to face is the move away from people working for the same employer for years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Instead, more and more people are becoming self-employed, to gain the freedom and control over their lives that they’re unlikely to get from being employed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: OK, well that’s all I want to say, so let’s open it up for discussion.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
